value.overview: The Curlew Sandpiper is a medium-sized migratory shorebird that breeds in the high Arctic tundra of northern Siberia and migrates to coastal and inland wetlands across Africa, southern Asia, Australia, and parts of the Pacific. It is recognized by its long, slightly down-curved bill, relatively long legs, and slim body. In breeding plumage it has rich reddish underparts; in nonbreeding plumage it is mostly gray and white. It is an uncommon to rare visitor in the Americas, including Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Curlew Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae and the genus Calidris. Its scientific name is Calidris ferruginea.
value.identification: A Curlew Sandpiper is slightly larger and longer-legged than a Dunlin, with a distinctive down-curved bill, long wings, and a smoothly rounded head. Nonbreeding adults are gray above, white below, and often show a pale eyebrow and dark streaking on the breast. Juveniles have neatly scaled upperparts. Breeding adults are strongly marked, with brick-red to chestnut underparts and dark-spotted upperparts. Care is needed because it can resemble Dunlin, Stilt Sandpiper, and other Calidris sandpipers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds mainly on Arctic tundra in northern Siberia and winters around shallow coastal wetlands, tidal mudflats, estuaries, saltmarshes, lagoons, and occasionally inland marshes. In Costa Rica, the Curlew Sandpiper is a very uncommon, irregular visitor rather than a regular abundant migrant. Reliable records are associated with suitable wetland or coastal habitats, especially muddy margins and shallow water where shorebirds feed. Any Costa Rican sighting is notable and should be documented carefully because confusion with similar Calidris species is possible.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most birds leave Arctic breeding grounds for Africa, southern Asia, Australia, and nearby regions. In Costa Rica it occurs only rarely and irregularly, probably as an unusual migrant or nonbreeding visitor, rather than as a predictable seasonal species.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place during the short Arctic summer, generally in open tundra near shallow pools, wet hollows, and low vegetation. The nest is a shallow depression lined with plant material, usually placed on the ground. The female commonly lays about four eggs, and both adults may participate in incubation and care of the young. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and forage independently while being guarded by the adults. The species forms breeding colonies or loose concentrations where suitable tundra habitat is available.
value.dietFeeding: Curlew Sandpipers feed mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, insect larvae, worms, mollusks, crustaceans, and other aquatic organisms. They forage by walking through shallow water or soft mud and probing with the bill. On tidal flats they may feed during falling or low tides, while at inland wetlands they use muddy edges and shallow pools. During migration and the nonbreeding season, they often feed in flocks, sometimes with Dunlins and other shorebirds.
value.behavior: This species is active and social outside the breeding season, often gathering in flocks that may include other sandpipers. It walks steadily while probing mud and shallow water, and it readily takes flight when disturbed. Flocks can wheel rapidly in coordinated formations. Curlew Sandpipers are generally quiet on wintering grounds but give short calls during flight or alarm. They must make repeated long-distance movements between breeding, staging, and nonbreeding areas, making them dependent on a chain of suitable wetlands.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing. Recent assessments indicate a decline of more than 30 percent over three generations, with some monitoring programs showing steeper reductions in particular regions.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss and degradation of tidal flats, estuaries, marshes, and other wetlands along migration routes and in nonbreeding areas. Disturbance at feeding and roosting sites, hunting in parts of the flyway, climate-related changes affecting Arctic breeding conditions, and reduced food availability may also contribute to the decline. Because Costa Rica receives the species only rarely, protecting coastal wetlands and maintaining accurate records are especially important for understanding its occurrence there.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore coastal mudflats, estuaries, saltmarshes, lagoons, and inland wetlands used by migratory shorebirds. Reduce disturbance near high-tide roosts and feeding areas by keeping dogs controlled, avoiding sensitive flocks, and following access restrictions. Support wetland conservation and responsible shorebird monitoring in Costa Rica and along international migration routes. Photograph and report unusual Curlew Sandpiper sightings to local bird-record committees or established citizen-science databases, including location, date, habitat, and identification details.
